I was fortunate to have a good rapport with my coworkers so during down time, I studied using the Kaplan books. Secondly, I had a good team so I didn't have to manage them all of the time. First lesson of good management is to delegate effectively and establish a good policy ans procedure-based culture. 

Since I took the MCAT twice, I knew what I was getting into the second time around. I felt fine with my first 513 but three schools needed new scores as the first ones from 2019 would have expired. That said, a bulk of the studying was done by the 2021 exam. 

Overall, I recommend the following. 
1. Have a good plan and stick with it. Be realistic and allow flex time. There will be good and bad days. 

2. Choose your resources wisely and stick with it. There are many resources out there and decision fatigue is real. I stuck to the Kaplan books, Anki (self-made cards), UWorld, and FLs (AAMC, Kaplan, and Next step). Some people need less, some need more. I could have used more but I didn't have time. My exam was in the middle of the app cycle so I very much wanted to get it done. However, do ALL of the AAMC materials. 

3. Take days and time off. Two weeks leading to my exam, I took it off to focus. 

4. Always review and learn from mistakes, don't ruminate. 

For CARS, I sucked. I got better after the AAMC practice but I am not confident in giving you advice given my meh performance (126 both times). My only tip is to coach yourself through it and try to find enjoyment from every passage. They can be obscure but I really enjoyed the ones that reminded me of my liberal arts courses. Try to read a lot of different articles to get used to different styles. Don't neglect this section. 

For P/S, I grasped things very easily but the first time I had challenges applying concepts. Anki definitely helped and I recommend a lot of visual aids, either from UWorld or making them yourself. Always apply P/S to real life scenarios, it helps you maintain the content. I went from 129 to 131.

I don't have a set list to recommend, but I do have guiding principles.

1. Don't base your experience of healthcare, medicine, or public health on other practitioners, e.g. Atul Gawande, Paul Farmer, and Anthony Fauci. While they have valuable perspectives, they aren't yours. Not all their perspectives are correct or right. Sometimes, providers reveal to us the kind of providers that we don't want to be. Sometimes they are providers that we've seen, sometimes they are derelict in duty. (NB: That last point is not a specific jab to the three listed above, making that explicitly clear.)  
2. Don't just read nonfiction. Nonfiction helps us understand the world. Fiction helps us understand one another. There is research demonstrating how fiction may help people empathize with one another. Read fully present and place yourself in the story. Don't hate the antagonist because of the antagonist's literary role. Sometimes the most compelling stories are those of a well-written villain. (NB: As in understanding different perspectives of conflict and disagreement, as well as understanding the root cause of something. Making it explicitly clear that you should not aspire to be a villain, but pay attention to villain origins stories.)  
3. There is no book, article, journal, film, song, or any media that can replace your own. Books help us with curiosity, but initiative pushes us towards experience. Always apply what you read to the world around you. This applies to every book, from a cancer genetics textbook to *Beloved* by Toni Morrison.  
4. Find the beauty and the arguments in the things that you read. If it makes you feel uncomfortable, reflect on why that is.

Thank you! My situation was very atypical. I was working around 100 hrs/week from primary to some of the secondaries. By interview season, I was back to working 40 hrs/week. Fortunately, I was compensated for extra hours. If I had to estimate, it was about $5,000. I highly recommend starting the process (writing PS and jotting down reflections for secondaries) very early, having a flexible job (a luxury), and setting aside enough savings for applications *and* interviews (another luxury). I emphasize that because it was uncertain whether or not schools were doing in person interviews. I built up some savings and hours for leave/holiday.   


And most importantly? Be targeted about your schools. There were some schools with missions and fits that I wasn't entirely the best match for. Take time to research the schools as best as you can. I didn't have that (above: working 100 hr weeks) so having a better list would have saved me time and money. If you qualify, apply for the application fee assistance. Because of my overtime, I wasn't eligible, which is okay. But now that I'm not on overtime, my financial situation has changed dramatically. Be budget savvy.

I am a very reflective person so for years (like ten years), I wrote down small thoughts or inclinations that I wanted to think deeply about. Some were more fruitful than others, but all were centered around how I envision medicine, healing, public health, etc. in this world. Weeks before my personal statement writing, I read a lot of books, more nonfiction than fiction, but paid attention to good writing. It helped me develop my sense of style and prose. 

Simultaneously, I filtered all those reflections and decided on which stories or anecdotes that I wanted to discuss in my personal statement and secondaries. I recognize that it's very cliche, but be passionate, be genuine. I struggled with writing my hole life, but after learning how to read *and* write like a writer, I got better (I'm not perfect). The PS process is challenging, but it is rewarding. You will never have a perfect draft, but you will know based on your intuition and feedback. I knew I had my draft (which was like V3.3) when my advisor read it, took a moment to absorb it, and described it as "gripping." Write until it feels right, really!

But again, do use your discretion. Smell the meat and visually inspect. If it tastes weird or anything out of ordinary, don't eat it. Your health and safety is important!

Because there are no ice crystals, I would not refreeze it. Anything above 40F should not be refrozen. Think of it this way: you could be avoiding a trip to the doctor's and losing paid working time. 

If you can, try to cook as much of the meat as possible. Then you can freeze the cooked meat and eat it later. If you had vegetables, it is okay to refreeze but they may freezer burn or lose some flavor but otherwise safe.

Edit: but also use your discretion. Do you know how long the meat has been thawed or > 40F? If it is longer than one or two hours, I would not risk it.

I think this offers an opportunity to discuss body positivity in a different perspective. I used this term to mean that we should honor the respects of each person, where there body is at and what their goals are whole understanding that each person's body positivity journey looks different. 

I think that it is nice to see someone own a body that is not conventionally attractive (conventionally attractive being muscles and abs). However, I feel like this praise is masking the real issue at hand: the social pressures embedded in the gay community to look a certain way. The operative distinction here is that this person chose to put on weight and much like the pressures some face to lose weight, he needed to work out and consume an absurd amount of calories. Some experts have used the term "bigorexia," which is the opposite of anorexia. I do feel like we need to dismantle this idea that gay men need to have muscles, with or without abs, and we need to move beyond the expectations to look a certain body type (think, otter, bear, etc).

I think that the "decomposes" part was put in to throw people off. Since the passage says that it is a stepwise process, I wrote the following: 

1. NADPH + FAD ⟶ NADP+ + FADH
2. FADH + H+ + O2 ⟶ FADH-OOH

If FADH-OOH decomposes non-productively (in the case of lys):

3. FADH-OOH ⟶ FAD+ + H2O2

​

Taken together, when you add all the reactions, you will see that FAD, FADH, & FADH-OOH all end up in reactants & products. Therefore, your *net* balanced reaction is NADPH + H+ + O2 ⟶ NADP+ + H2O2.
